primary.title: Rosen Contacted Manhattan Prosecutors After Manafort’s Lawyer Raised Rikers Concerns
primary.description_short: Jeffrey Rosen sought Manhattan prosecutors’ views after Manafort’s lawyer asked that he remain in federal custody over Rikers concerns.
primary.description_medium: NBC News reported that Paul Manafort’s lawyer asked federal officials to keep him in federal custody because of health and safety concerns about Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen sent Manhattan prosecutors the lawyer’s letter and asked for their views. Their office said it made no housing recommendation; Manafort stayed in federal custody in Manhattan.
primary.description_long: In June 2019, as Manhattan prosecutors prepared a state case against Paul Manafort, his lawyer asked the Bureau of Prisons to keep him in federal custody, citing health and personal-safety concerns about Rikers Island. NBC News obtained a letter Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen sent to Manhattan prosecutors with the defense letter attached; Rosen asked whether the office had a response. District Attorney Cyrus Vance replied that his office had made no recommendation about where Manafort should be housed and took no position among Rikers, another city facility, or the Metropolitan Correctional Center. Federal officials ultimately kept Manafort in federal custody at the Manhattan facility while making him available to state prosecutors. The reporting supports DOJ involvement after a defense request, followed by consultation with prosecutors and a stated health-and-safety rationale. It does not establish that DOJ independently ordered Manafort kept out of Rikers, that prosecutors opposed the arrangement, or that President Trump directed the decision. The prior title’s claim of a Trump DOJ order therefore overstates the documented sequence.
primary.date_precision: day; federal officials informed Manhattan prosecutors on Monday, June 17, 2019, as reported by NBC News on June 18.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Court-Martial Generals Who Criticized Him
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, Trump publicly threatened to seek court-martials for retired generals who had spoken critically of him, including former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Mark Milley and former Defense Secretary James Mattis. The threats represented an extraordinary attempt to use military law to silence civilian critics who had once served in uniform. Legal experts noted that retired officers retain First Amendment rights and cannot be court-martialed for speech made after leaving service. The threats were widely condemned as an attempt to intimidate the military brass and chill any future dissent from senior officers.

frozen_original.title: Trump Administration Revokes Visas of Dozens of Harvard Students
frozen_original.synopsis: In May 2025, in retaliation for Harvard University's refusal to comply with the administration's demands, the Trump administration revoked the student and exchange visitor visas of dozens of current Harvard students, leaving them unable to legally remain in or re-enter the United States. Harvard enrolled approximately 6,800 international students, and the targeted revocations were described by university officials as arbitrary and punitive. Students who received revocation notices included those with no history of protest activity, apparently targeted simply for their enrollment at a defiant institution. Harvard filed an emergency legal challenge. The action was the first time in modern American history that a presidential administration had used visa revocations as a tool to punish a university for institutional resistance to executive demands.

primary.title: Trump Issues Harvard Entry Suspension; Current Visa Revocations Remain Under Consideration
primary.description_short: A June 4 proclamation suspended entry for some incoming Harvard students and only called for discretionary review of current visas.
primary.description_medium: On June 4, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation suspending entry for certain nonimmigrant students seeking to begin study at Harvard through SEVP, with exceptions and a stated six-month duration. It separately directed the Secretary of State to consider whether some current Harvard students’ visas should be revoked. That instruction did not establish that current students’ visas had already been canceled. A later temporary court order blocked the policy, according to Harvard Gazette.
primary.description_long: On June 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation suspending entry for nonimmigrants seeking to begin a course of study at Harvard through the Student and Exchange Visitor Program. The proclamation set a six-month period unless extended and included exceptions; it also said the restriction did not apply to students entering to attend other universities through the program. Separately, it directed the Secretary of State to consider, in the Secretary’s discretion, whether certain current Harvard students with F, M, or J visas should have them revoked. That wording authorized a review; it does not say that visas belonging to dozens of current students had already been canceled. The proclamation stated national-security concerns and alleged Harvard had failed to provide records about foreign students. Harvard Gazette reported that University officials denied that allegation and that DHS had moved in May to pull Harvard’s certification. The Gazette also reported a temporary court order issued June 5 blocking the administration’s plan. This supported entry covers the June 4 proclamation and separates it from the earlier certification dispute and April SEVIS record terminations. The number of students affected by those separate actions remains unresolved.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

That suspension and limitation shall expire, absent extension, 6 months after the date of this proclamation.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The entry of any alien into the United States as a nonimmigrant to pursue a course of study at Harvard University under section 101(a)(15)(F) or section 101(a)(15)(M) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(F) or 101(a)(15)(M), or to participate in an exchange visitor program hosted by Harvard University under section 101(a)(15)(J) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(J), is suspended and limited, subject to section 2 of this proclamation. That suspension and limitation shall expire, absent extension, 6 months after the date of this proclamation.

source_fact_map.fact: The proclamation directed discretionary consideration of revoking some current students’ visas; it did not report completed revocations.
source_fact_map.quote: The Secretary of State shall consider, in the Secretary’s discretion, whether foreign nationals who currently attend Harvard University
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The Secretary of State shall consider, in the Secretary’s discretion, whether foreign nationals who currently attend Harvard University and are in the United States pursuant to F, M, or J visas and who otherwise meet the criteria described in section 1 of this proclamation should have their visas revoked pursuant to section 221(i) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1201(i).

source_fact_map.fact: Harvard Gazette reported a DHS move in May to pull Harvard’s certification and said University officials denied the records allegation.

source_fact_map.fact: Harvard Gazette reported a temporary order issued June 5 after the proclamation.
source_fact_map.quote: The ruling extends a temporary order issued June 5
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The ruling extends a temporary order issued June 5, one day after a proclamation by President Trump declaring that the federal government would deny visas to international students headed to Harvard.
